newsitem.title: USA: Columbia/HCA, Value Health revise merger.
newsitem.headline: Columbia/HCA, Value Health revise merger.

text.p: Columbia/HCA Healthcare Corp. and Value Health Inc. Tuesday revised the financial terms of their proposed merger to compensate for a recent steep decline in Columbia/HCA's stock price.
Under the new plan, stockholders of Value Health will receive $20.50 in cash for each share in a transaction valued at $1.2 billion.
First announced in January, the original deal was a $1.3 billion stock swap that called for each Value Health share to be exchanged for 0.58 shares of Columbia common stock.

But the value of the transaction had fallen to about $995 million in recent weeks due to news of a federal probe into Columbia's billing practices. Columbia, which owns and operates more than 340 hospitals and other healthcare facilities, is based in Nashville, Tenn.

"I think the uncertainty of what's happening in the stock is a reason. We wanted to take as much uncertainty out of the deal for our shareholders as was possible," said Value Health spokeswoman Judith Hyfield-Starr.
The original deal did not have a provision to protect Value Health shareholders in case of a decline in Columbia's stock price, Hyfield-Starr said.
Value Health, based in Avon, Conn., said other terms of the revised deal were essentially unchanged.

Value Health said its board of directors approved the revised transaction with Columbia as being in the best interests of the company's stockholders. The deal, which remains subject to the approval of shareholders and regulators, is expected to be completed in the second quarter.
ValueHealth previously had rejected an offer from MedPartners Inc. which had proposed its own stock swap in January.
Value Health's stock gained $2.25 to close at $20, while Columbia/HCA rose $2.75 to $34.125 on the New York Stock Exchange.
Also Tuesday, Columbia said its board has authorised a $1 billion stock repurchase programme, represening about 5 percent of its shares.

The original stock transaction with Value Health was to be accounted for as a pooling of interests. Companies participating in a pooling are prohibited from participating in stock repurchase programmes.
"They're taking advantage of the stock drop to repurchase some shares so I think that's a good move," said Brian Eisenbarth of Collins & Co.

Columbia stock, which was trading at about $40 per share in January when the Value Health deal originally was announced, has fallen sharply due to concerns about the federal probe. The health care company has said it is cooperating with federal agents and has not been informed of allegations.

Value Health provides speciality benefit programmes to large corporations, insurance carriers, managed care organisations, and government agencies. Programmes include pharmacy benefit management; mental health and substance abuse management; workers' compensation, disability and group health management; and disease management.
